doc.title: Ray Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, AZ, April 16, 2000

chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and the Oscar Peterson Trio
title: Pranks with Oscar Peterson and Norman Granz in Japan
summary: Brown tells of the Ballad Medley, the detuned bass before Ella Fitzgerald, and his revenge with pachinko balls in the piano.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Yeah. You guys seem to have no lack of sense of humor in the Oscar Peterson Trio. Is that a fair statement?
Well when we were young we did a lot of crazy things. I think everybody does. Nobody has a corner on that. If we all go back to when we were young, we carried on.
I suppose you’ve read some of the anecdotes in the Bill Crow book.
Some of them are pretty close, yeah.
There was one, something about Bill Harris who purposely knocked over something when Oscar was trying to sing or something like that?

Yeah but that was the backlash of something that happened before. We were in Japan and we used to have something called a Ballad Medley. The Ballad Medley was everybody playing one chorus of whatever ballad he chose to play. So what they did is they would black out the stage, put a spotlight just in the front at the microphone. The first guy would walk out, he would walk past Oscar and he’d say “’I’ve Got It Bad’ B flat” and then he’d

walk over. As he’s walking to the mic Oscar would do a four or eight bar introduction. He’d play one chorus. And then as he’s walking off to applause, the next guy walked by and Oscar would say so-and-so-and-so. And that’s the Ballad Medley. Okay. Now all of these tricks and stuff are still going on. I used to lay my bass on the stage, because we’d have a break at intermission, and then we would start the second half with Ella Fitzgerald. So they would call Buddy Rich, Herb Ellis, Ray Brown, Oscar Peterson, and they’d say and Ella Fitzgerald. And she would come out and we would play as she was coming out. Well this night in Japan Oscar Peterson and Norman Granz got together and they went over and they tuned all my strings down see. Then when it’s time to start, Norman Granz says, “Now ladies and gentlemen for the second set, Buddy Rich on drums, he goes out; Herb Ellis on guitar; Oscar Peterson on piano; Ray Brown on bass; and Ella Fitzgerald. Now so we practically came out at the same time. So these guys are starting when I got to my bass. And I pick it up and she’s out there, and I go — and the strings are like limp. And she’s trying to sing and I’m back there going [scats]. And she looks back — what? And I look at Oscar Peterson and he’s got that look I know he’s part of it see. Then I look in the wings and I see Norman Granz holding his side. They’re just laughing away. Okay. So now in between shows I go out and I walk into some little Japanese joint down the street and there’s something called Pachinko and it’s little steel balls about this big, about the tip of your finger say, little round balls. And they go up in the machine and they come down in holes. So I played this thing for about fifteen minutes and I didn’t win but there was a bunch of balls. And I put about thirty of them in my pocket. I go back to the theater. When they turned the lights out for the ballad medley, I reached in my pocket and I strung all these balls next to the hammers on the piano. So now the first guy to come out for the ballad medley is Bill Harris. And told Oscar so-and-so-and-so-and-so. And he goes to the mic and starts playing. Oscar hits the piano and it goes [scats] and it sounds like a calliope. So he’s looking at me, what the hell? So that’s how I got even with Oscar Peterson. So you see how those —
So Oscar started it and the whole thing came in a big circle.
